land.text: most Tianwan territories (Chen Han page), Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi

predecessors.note: Infobox Preceded by: Yuan dynasty; the state is Tianwan's general Chen Youliang's coup of 1360.

land.text: Zhu occupied and absorbed the Han territories in Hubei, Hunan, and Jiangxi by April 1365

successors.note: Infobox Succeeded by: Zhu Yuanzhang's state of Wu. Jiangxi had passed to Zhu in 1362.

capitals.name: Jiujiang
capitals.note: Infobox Jiujiang, later Wuchang; early 1360 declared himself King of Han with his capital at Jiujiang (approximate modern city position)

capitals.name: Wuchang (Wuhan)
capitals.note: After the failed attack on Nanjing in 1360 Chen withdrew to Wuchang, which he made his capital (Red Turban page); the page gives no month, so the dot moves in 1361

rulers.name: Chen Youliang
rulers.title: emperor of the Great Han

rulers.name: Chen Li
rulers.title: emperor
rulers.note: Surrendered Wuchang in March 1364; sent to Korea in 1372.

correction.text: Chen proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Han and took most Tianwan territories; Zhu occupied and absorbed the Han territories in Hubei, Hunan, and Jiangxi (Chen Han page): the whole of the former Tianwan land

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The infobox gives no area (Area: not given), so there is no figure to compare. Jiujiang and Anqing changed hands more than once in 1361 (ledger); the shape keeps Jiangxi to the surrender of Nanchang in early 1362.

New keyframe. Early 1362 (Nanchang): Han garrison commander Hu Mei surrendered Nanchang to Zhu, giving Zhu control of Jiangxi, which leaves Hubei and Hunan; Wuchang withstood a two-month siege after Chen Youliang's death and surrendered in March 1364, while the absorption of the rest lasted until April 1365.

region.text: Jiujiang in northern Jiangxi, 'his own domain in northern Jiangxi' (1357) and the Han capital in early 1360

ledger.note: Early 1360: Chen Youliang declares himself King of Han at Jiujiang. Chen declared himself King of Han with his capital at Jiujiang; he had 'established his own domain in northern Jiangxi' in 1357 after the failed plot of Ni Wenjun.

region.text: Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi, the Tianwan territories

ledger.note: June 1360: Chen murders Xu Shouhui and takes Tianwan's land. Chen proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Han and took most Tianwan territories; the Tianwan page says he attacked Hanyang in June and killed Xu with most of the court.
June 1360: Chen Youliang proclaims himself emperor of the Great Han. 'He subsequently declared himself emperor of the Great Han' after the earlier title King of Han.

region.text: the middle Yangtze and Lake Poyang between Anqing, Jiujiang and Nanchang, where Chen and Zhu fought in 1361-1363

ledger.note: 1361: Han and Wu fight over the Yangtze at Jiujiang and Anqing. Zhu had captured Jiujiang earlier that year, the Han retook Jiujiang and Anqing in August, and Zhu's fleet took Jiujiang again in September.
1361: Zhu captures Jiujiang. The Chen Han page says only that Zhu had captured Jiujiang earlier that year (before August 1361).

August 1361: the Han retake Jiujiang and Anqing. Han forces retook Jiujiang and Anqing after Zhu had captured Jiujiang earlier that year. Only Jiujiang is mapped (Anqing in Anhui lies outside the Han shape and the page does not say what became of it).
September 1361: Zhu's fleet defeats the Han fleet and takes Jiujiang for good; it fails to take Hanyang. Zhu's fleet defeated the Han fleet, captured Jiujiang, and failed to take Hanyang.

September 1361: with Jiujiang lost, Chen Youliang holds out at Wuchang, his capital to 1364. Chen Han page: in September 1361 Zhu's forces defeated the Han fleet before Jiujiang and captured the city; Zhu captured Jiujiang and blocked the remaining forces of Chen Youliang in Wuchang. The Red Turban page puts the withdrawal to Wuchang right after the failed attack on Nanjing (1360) without a year. Moved from 1360 to 1361 by reviewer ea-06-x to agree with identity.capitals (Wuchang 1361-1364) and the Chen Han page.
Early 1362: Nanchang surrenders and Zhu holds Jiangxi. Han garrison commander Hu Mei surrendered Nanchang to Zhu, giving Zhu control of Jiangxi.

region.text: the middle Yangtze and Lake Poyang between Anqing, Jiujiang and Nanchang, where Chen and Zhu fought in 1361-1363

ledger.note: March 1364: the fighting ends at Wuchang. After Chen Youliang was killed at Lake Poyang (3 October 1363) his son Chen Li withstood a two-month siege of Wuchang and surrendered in March 1364.

March 1364: Chen Li surrenders Wuchang and the Han ends. Chen Li surrendered, ending the state; Zhu then occupied and absorbed the Han territories until April 1365, with Xu Da pacifying Huguang (Hongwu Emperor page).

wars.name: Chen Youliang's war with Zhu Yuanzhang (Battle of Lake Poyang)

zones.text: the middle Yangtze and Lake Poyang between Anqing, Jiujiang and Nanchang, where Chen and Zhu fought in 1361-1363

wars.outcome: Zhu wins: Jiujiang 1361, Jiangxi 1362, the Battle of Lake Poyang (30 August to 3 October 1363, Chen killed by an arrow), Wuchang surrenders March 1364 and the Han lands are absorbed by April 1365.
wars.note: Han attack on Nanjing in 1360 repelled; Chen is said to have gathered 300,000 men in 1363 while Zhu was busy in Anhui, against about 100,000 under Zhu.

wars.name: Red Turban Rebellions
wars.outcome: Umbrella conflict; Zhu absorbs most rebel states and proclaims the Ming in 1368.
wars.note: Listed for completeness; the territorial fighting of this state is the war above.

certainty.note: River and lake frontiers held by fleets; no page gives a boundary line.

notes: Written for ea-06-x from the Chen Han page (infobox and dated list), with the Red Turban Rebellions page for the Wuchang capital and the Tianwan page for the murder of Xu. Cliopatria has no row, so both keyframes are new: Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi until early 1362, Hubei and Hunan afterwards. The Red Turban page's line that Chen's state took Chongqing and held all of Sichuan in 1357-1359 is not used: the Tianwan and Ming Xia pages give Sichuan to Ming Yuzhen. Anqing (retaken in August 1361) is in the contest zone but not in the shape; the page does not say how long the Han held it. The infobox gives no area. The Hongwu Emperor page puts the Han absorption in 1364-1365 (Xu Da pacifying Huguang); the dissolve is dated to the surrender of Wuchang. Counterparts needing dossiers: zhu-yuanzhang-s-wu (this batch), tianwan (this batch).
